questions.prompt: Name the two main families of matter particles in the Standard Model.
questions.answer: The main matter-particle families are quarks and leptons.

questions.prompt: What is a hadron?
questions.answer: A hadron is a composite particle made from quarks, held together by the strong interaction.

questions.prompt: State the quark content of a baryon and of a meson.
questions.answer: A baryon is made from three quarks, \(qqq\). A meson is made from a quark and an antiquark, \(q\bar q\).

questions.prompt: Why is an electron classified as a lepton rather than a hadron?
questions.answer: An electron is not made of quarks and does not experience the strong interaction, so it is a lepton.

questions.prompt: What is an antiparticle?
questions.answer: An antiparticle has the same rest mass as its corresponding particle but opposite charge and opposite additive quantum numbers such as lepton number or baryon number.

questions.prompt: Find the charge of a proton from its quark content \(uud\).
questions.answer:
\[
Q=+\frac23+\frac23-\frac13=+1
\]
So the proton has charge \(+e\).

questions.prompt: Find the charge of a neutron from its quark content \(udd\).
questions.answer:
\[
Q=+\frac23-\frac13-\frac13=0
\]
So the neutron is electrically neutral.

questions.prompt: Why does a meson have baryon number zero?
questions.answer: A meson contains one quark with \(B=+1/3\) and one antiquark with \(B=-1/3\), so the total baryon number is zero.

questions.prompt: Classify a pion as a baryon, meson, lepton, or exchange boson.
questions.answer: A pion is a meson because it is made from a quark-antiquark pair.

questions.prompt: Find the charge of a \(u\bar d\) meson.
questions.answer: The up quark has charge \(+2/3\) and the anti-down quark has charge \(+1/3\). The total is \(+1\), so the meson has charge \(+e\).

questions.prompt: Explain why charge conservation alone is not enough to decide whether a particle reaction is allowed.
questions.answer: Allowed reactions must also conserve energy, momentum, angular momentum, baryon number, lepton number, and any other relevant quantum numbers. Charge conservation is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.prompt: A particle has baryon number \(+1\) and is made of quarks. What family is it in?
questions.answer: It is a baryon. Baryons are hadrons made from three quarks and have baryon number \(+1\).

questions.prompt: A particle has lepton number \(+1\) and no quark content. What broad classification is most likely?
questions.answer: It is most likely a lepton, such as an electron, muon, tau, or neutrino.

questions.prompt: Why do antiparticles have the same rest mass as their particles?
questions.answer: Particle-antiparticle pairs are related by fundamental symmetries of the theory. They differ in charge-like quantum numbers, not in rest mass.

questions.prompt: Use baryon number to explain why a proton cannot simply decay into a positron and a photon in the Standard Model.
questions.answer: The proton has baryon number \(+1\). A positron and a photon have baryon number \(0\). Baryon number would not be conserved, so this decay is forbidden in the Standard Model.

questions.prompt: A reaction has one proton initially and only mesons finally. What baryon-number issue arises?
questions.answer: The initial baryon number is \(+1\). Mesons have baryon number \(0\), so the final baryon number would be \(0\). The reaction violates baryon-number conservation as written.

questions.prompt: Find the charge and baryon number of an antibaryon made from \(\bar u\bar u\bar d\).
questions.answer: The charge is \(-2/3-2/3+1/3=-1\). Each antiquark has baryon number \(-1/3\), so the total baryon number is \(-1\).

questions.prompt: Why are neutrinos placed with leptons even though they are neutral?
questions.answer: They are not made from quarks, carry lepton number, and participate in weak interactions. Electric neutrality does not make them hadrons.

questions.prompt: A final state contains a baryon-antibaryon pair. What is the net baryon number of the pair?
questions.answer: The baryon has \(B=+1\) and the antibaryon has \(B=-1\). The pair has net baryon number \(0\).

questions.prompt: Explain why particle families are useful in predicting unknown particles.
questions.answer: Family patterns reveal missing combinations and conservation-law structures. If related particles form a pattern, an unobserved member can be predicted by its expected charge, mass scale, and decay behaviour.
